articles.title: Cardinal Langley RC High School wins award for commitment to sport
articles.excerpt: Cardinal Langley RC High School in Middleton has been awarded for its dedication to sports and inclusivity in education.
articles.content_html:
Cardinal Langley RC High School in Middleton has been recognised for its commitment to sports, winning the Outstanding Commitment to Sport in Secondary School category at the Educate Awards 2026 held in Liverpool.

The school's physical education department impressed judges with its extensive extra-curricular and competitive sports programme, which has enabled over 100 students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) to participate in activities such as boccia, panathlon, and new age kurling.

Helen Farrell, a sixth form ambassador at the school, was also named runner-up in the School Support Star of the Year category for her dedication to supporting students.

Cardinal Langley was recognised as a runner-up in two other categories, including Outstanding SEND Provision in Mainstream School.

articles.title: Alan Thomson extradited from Dubai to face organised crime charges in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Alan Thomson, 46, has been extradited from Dubai to face charges related to a drug operation in Rochdale and Glasgow.
articles.content_html:
Alan Thomson, 46, has been extradited from Dubai to Scotland to face charges of organised crime, including running a drug operation that allegedly spanned Glasgow and Rochdale between March and June 2020.

Thomson appeared at Glasgow Sheriff Court alongside co-accused Mohamed Eldirani, 55. Both men made no plea during their initial court appearance and were remanded in custody.

The charges against Thomson include directing others to sell and supply drugs such as cannabis, cocaine, and diamorphine, as well as managing the collection and transportation of criminal proceeds. The extradition followed a joint investigation involving the National Crime Agency and authorities in the UAE.

The allegations highlight the ongoing issue of cross-border drug trafficking affecting communities in both Scotland and England, including areas in Greater Manchester.

articles.title: Rochdale primary schools launch engineering programme for pupils
articles.excerpt: Ten primary schools in Rochdale have begun a new engineering initiative to inspire students through hands-on learning and professional interaction.
articles.content_html:
Ten primary schools in Rochdale have launched a new initiative aimed at inspiring the next generation of engineers through hands-on learning. Staff from these schools participated in a continuous professional development (CPD) training day to implement the Primary Engineer Vehicle Programme.

The programme allows pupils to build and test their own vehicle models while interacting with engineering professionals. At the end of the programme, students will celebrate their achievements at a joint school event, showcasing their projects.

Rochdale Council, in partnership with Rochdale Development and Primary Engineers, is facilitating this initiative. The programme includes a full day of CPD training, high-quality kits, and classroom resources, enabling 60 pupils at each school to construct 15 shoebox locomotives and 15 motorised locomotives.

This year marks the first collaboration between these organisations, with the aim of fostering interest in STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) subjects among young learners in Rochdale.

articles.title: Marios Plus Pizzeria rated 1 out of 5 for food hygiene
articles.excerpt: Marios Plus Pizzeria, a takeaway or sandwich shop at 8 Wood Street, Middleton, Manchester, M24 5TF, has been given a food hygiene rating of 1 out of 5, meaning major improvement is necessary, after an inspection on 20 October 2026.
articles.content_html:
Marios Plus Pizzeria, a takeaway or sandwich shop at 8 Wood Street, Middleton, Manchester, M24 5TF, has been given a food hygiene rating of 1 out of 5, meaning major improvement is necessary, after an inspection on 20 October 2026.

The rating appears on the Food Standards Agency's public register for the Rochdale borough, checked by Rochdale Daily on 27 November 2026. A low rating is usually published only after the business's 21-day appeal period has passed, so it appears some weeks after the inspection.

Under the national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme, councils score businesses from 0, where urgent improvement is necessary, to 5, where hygiene standards are very good.

The score reflects how food was handled, the condition of the premises and how food safety was managed on the day of the inspection. It is not a judgement of the quality of the food.

64 food businesses in the borough currently hold a rating of 0 or 1, according to the same register.

A business can appeal its rating, publish a right of reply alongside it on the Food Standards Agency website, and ask for a re-inspection once improvements have been made, so the rating may since have changed. The current rating is at https://ratings.food.gov.uk/business/802265.

articles.title: NHS asks Rochdale families to help get patients home safely from hospital this winter
articles.excerpt: Families and friends are being asked to be ready to collect loved ones, prepare their homes and speak to ward teams early as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families are being asked to help relatives leave hospital safely this winter as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.

NHS England says hospitals and community services across the region are working to make sure patients can leave hospital as soon as they are well enough. Families and friends can help by being ready to collect their loved ones when the time comes.

Returning to familiar surroundings with the right support in place can help people recover, regain their independence and get back to their usual routines. Staying in hospital longer than needed can increase the risk of infection and loss of strength and mobility.

Dr Michael Gregory, Regional Medical Director for NHS England in the North West, said: “For patients, going home is about getting back to the people and everyday life they know. This is something that can make a real difference to recovery. Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.

“If you are worried about how someone will manage, please speak to the ward team early. We want to understand those concerns and what help you can offer, so we can plan together for a safe return home.”

Ward teams will work with patients and, where appropriate, their family, friends or unpaid carers to plan a safe discharge. They will discuss what support may be available and how to access it, and will aim for discharge earlier in the day where possible.

Before leaving, patients and those supporting them should understand the discharge plan, including any medicines, follow-up appointments and who to contact with concerns.

NHS England suggests families and friends check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.

Relatives can bring suitable clothes and shoes for the journey home, and check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.

At home, families can help by putting the heating on, making sure food and other essentials are available, and clearing walkways of clutter and trip hazards.

They should also make sure the patient knows who to contact if they need help.

Across the North West, specialist wards and services providing hospital-level care at home are helping patients leave hospital sooner. They include the Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary, a specialist dementia ward featured in the same NHS England campaign.

Anyone who needs urgent medical help after returning home and is unsure where to turn can contact NHS 111 by phone or at 111.nhs.uk. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

Source: NHS England North West press office, press release issued on 24 November 2026.

  • Families can check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.
  • Relatives can check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.

articles.title: Rochdale Infirmary dementia care scheme cuts hospital stays by up to eight days
articles.excerpt: Specialist dementia wards including Rochdale Infirmary’s Oasis Unit are helping patients return home sooner, with average stays reduced by up to eight days.
articles.content_html:
A specialist dementia care model used at Rochdale Infirmary is helping patients return home sooner, with average hospital stays across the programme reduced by up to eight days, NHS England says.

The Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary is one of three Northern Care Alliance services highlighted in a winter discharge campaign. Similar specialist dementia wards operate at Fairfield General Hospital in Bury and Salford Royal.

Patients living with dementia can remain on the same ward throughout their hospital stay, reducing moves that can be unsettling and allowing staff to provide care in a familiar environment. Activities are tailored to individual needs as part of the approach.

Northern Care Alliance information describes the Oasis Unit as a 10-bed medical ward for patients who have an acute medical condition and are also living with dementia. The unit includes colour-coordinated rooms and shared spaces designed to help with orientation and recovery.

NHS England said teams begin speaking with relatives early in a patient's stay and work with Age UK to arrange support for a safe return home. Across the specialist ward programme, the average length of stay has fallen by up to eight days.

Dr Michael Gregory, NHS England's Regional Medical Director for the North West, said: “Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.”

The NHS is asking relatives and carers to discuss practical arrangements with hospital teams before a patient is ready to leave. This can include transport, suitable clothing, food at home and help with follow-up appointments or medicines.

For Rochdale families, early discharge planning can reduce delays once a patient is medically ready to leave hospital and make the move home safer.

Sources: NHS England North West news release, 24 November 2026; Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, Oasis Unit patient information and Discharge Integration Frontrunner Programme.

articles.title: First Bus Rochdale wins national Gold for Routes to Work scheme
articles.excerpt: First Bus Rochdale’s employability programme has won Gold at the UK Bus Awards after helping local young people build skills and move into work.
articles.content_html:
First Bus Rochdale’s Routes to Work programme has won Gold in the Bus and the Community category at the 2026 UK Bus Awards, adding to the operator’s Community Engagement Award at the Rochdale Business Awards.

The national winners were announced in London on Tuesday 24 November. The UK Bus Awards named Routes to Work as the Gold winner ahead of schemes from First Bus West Yorkshire and Arriva Merseyside.

Routes to Work was created to help young people who are not in education, employment or training gain workplace experience, build confidence and prepare for jobs. Participants received practical experience at First Bus’s Rochdale depot alongside support with CVs, applications and interviews.

First Bus said the first programme involved four young people and that two had secured full-time work by October. One joined the engineering stores team at the Rochdale depot, while another found work with Rochdale firm Royton Steelstock.

The local Community Engagement Award recognised a wider year of work with schools, colleges, charities and community groups. First Bus was also shortlisted for Business of the Year at the Rochdale ceremony.

Zoe Hands, managing director of First Bus Franchising, said: “These awards belong to our colleagues and partners, whose passion and commitment help create opportunities for people across Rochdale every day.”

Kevin Mullin, social value manager at First Bus Rochdale, said the recognition reflected the combined work of staff, partners and volunteers supporting local people and strengthening community links.

For Rochdale residents, the award highlights a practical local route into employment for young people who may lack experience or established workplace contacts.

Sources: First Bus Corporate press office, 27 November 2026; UK Bus Awards 2026 results; Rochdale Development Agency.

articles.title: Who or what is the Healey Dwarf?
articles.excerpt: A small ginger‑bearded figure from Healey Dell’s storybooks is a local piece of nineteenth‑century folklore rather than a documented historical person.
articles.summary: A small ginger‑bearded figure from Healey Dell’s storybooks is a local piece of nineteenth‑century folklore rather than a documented historical person.
articles.body:
Stand on the path beside the River Spodden at Healey Dell and you can still picture the pocket‑sized companion who haunts the Dell’s visitor leaflets: the Healey Dwarf, usually described as the size of a child with a large ginger beard and green‑and‑brown clothes, who courts the Fairy Queen in the rock recess called the Fairies’ Chapel. This image is the product of a long tradition of oral tale and Victorian retelling; it is part of the reserve’s modern visitor interpretation rather than a recorded, verifiable historical person. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want the oldest printed witness to the story, look to the county folklorist John Roby. In his Traditions of Lancashire (first issued 1829–31) Roby printed a lengthy romance‑style account known as “The Fairies’ Chapel” that preserves the core plot elements that later writers and guides repeated: a rock “chapel” in the Thrutch, a set of fairy characters, a local fortune‑teller and wondrous incidents tied to the place. Roby was collecting and recording oral material; his pages are a nineteenth‑century retrieval of what people were already telling, not an archive of contemporary medieval records. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Victorian authors then dressed the tale in theatrical costume. An 1882 pamphlet‑book, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies by R. Standring, expands and romanticises the episode and is one clear source for the dwarf’s later cartoon‑like appearance (crimson waistcoat, checked trousers and that memorable ginger beard) that you’ll meet in modern retellings. Standring’s telling is literary invention built on Roby’s collected material rather than new documentary evidence. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Healey_Dell_Or_The_History_in_Verse_of_F.html?id=IYMNAAAAYAAJ))

Local interpretation today bundles those nineteenth‑century witnesses with the landscape itself. The heritage centre at Healey Dell prints and performs versions of the Fairy Chapel and Healey Dwarf stories for visitors, and the centre’s illustrated guides make plain that this is cultural memory and attraction writing rather than archival fact. The council’s visitor entry for Healey Dell lists the reserve’s address, facilities and history — the Dell’s waterfalls, mill remains and a visitor centre with a “Fairy Grotto” — and treats the tales as part of the site’s lore. Those stones, paths and the heritage centre are the verifiable things you can point a camera at; the supernatural cast of the story belongs to folklore. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

The place that fed the story is real and well recorded. The high, eight‑arched sandstone viaduct that spans the gorge is Grade II listed on the National Heritage List for England, and the Dell’s industrial archaeology and river‑cut features are documented in local records and guide material. It was the look of a narrow water‑cut alcove — once described as containing a natural “pulpit, reading desk and seats” before a violent 1838 flood altered the rock — that prompted people to call it the Fairies’ Chapel and to attach tales to it. Those are physical facts; the particulars of prophecies, fairy monarchies and a named medieval victim are not produced in contemporary church or court records within the nineteenth‑century sources that preserved the story. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

That separation matters for readers who enjoy the Dell’s stories but also like their history tidy. Treat Roby and Standring as early printed witnesses to local storytelling, and treat the Healey Dell Heritage Centre and Rochdale Council guides as how the tale is presented to visitors today. None of those sources produces contemporary medieval documents proving a living Healey Dwarf or a fairy prophecy as factual history; what they do show, clearly and attractively, is how landscape, industry and oral memory made a durable local legend. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

If you want to follow the trail yourself, read Roby’s “The Fairies’ Chapel” in his Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest printed account, compare the Victorian poem and pamphlets that followed, and look at the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s guides and the council’s visitor page when you plan a visit. The dwarf remains a good story to meet on a walk; the stones and the viaduct are what you will actually be standing beside. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

articles.content_html:
David Byrne, co-founder of Junction 21 Chauffeurs, was recently recognised as a finalist at the Rochdale Business Awards for his role in developing a UK-wide chauffeur directory. This directory aims to improve visibility and promote professional standards within the chauffeur and private hire industry.

The directory features over 100 licensed operators from across the UK, providing a simple way for users to locate licensed chauffeur services. It is designed to help businesses and travellers find operators with the appropriate licenses, ensuring compliance with industry standards.

Byrne expressed pride in being a finalist, highlighting the importance of the directory in raising awareness of professional standards in the sector. The sponsorship of the awards reflects Junction 21's commitment to economic development and support for local businesses.

The Rochdale Business Awards celebrate the achievements of local entrepreneurs and businesses, showcasing innovation and excellence in various sectors. Byrne's recognition alongside other business leaders underscores the impact of local enterprises on the broader economy.

Rochdale Borough Council has announced that the roadworks are necessary for repairs, although specific details about the nature of the repairs have not been disclosed. Residents and commuters are advised to plan alternative routes during this period.

For further information, residents can view a map of the roadworks on the Rochdale Borough Council website.

For people in Middleton

  • The closure will impact access to nearby roads including Boarshaw Road and Market Place.

articles.title: Parvez Qadir wins regional award for community impact in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Parvez Qadir, founder of Breaking Barriers, has received a regional award for his contributions to community cohesion in Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Parvez Qadir, founder of the community initiative Breaking Barriers, has been honoured with a regional award recognising his significant contributions to community cohesion in Greater Manchester.

The award celebrates individuals who have made a positive impact in their communities, highlighting Qadir's efforts since establishing Breaking Barriers in Rochdale in 2019.

Breaking Barriers has reached an impressive 655,000 people digitally, focusing on social issues and promoting understanding among diverse groups.

Qadir's projects, such as 'Crossing the Line' and 'Blind Side', have led to measurable increases in awareness regarding peer pressure and violence against women and girls (VAWG), with respective increases of 33% and 38% in understanding.

Expressing his gratitude, Qadir stated that he feels humbled to receive such recognition for his work. He aims to continue using creativity as a tool for social change, fostering a more inclusive community.

As he continues his work, Qadir hopes to inspire others to engage in community-building activities.

articles.title: Greater Manchester introduces AI-assisted traffic lights and new train services
articles.excerpt: The Bee Network in Greater Manchester is set to enhance transport with AI traffic lights and additional train services by the end of December.
articles.content_html:
The Greater Manchester transport network is undergoing significant changes, including the introduction of AI-assisted traffic lights and an expansion of train services. These updates are part of the Bee Network initiative aimed at improving public transport efficiency across the region.

Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that 70 additional train services will be added by the end of December, following a reduction of 230 services due to industrial action by the RMT union.

Danny Vaughan, Chief Network Officer at TfGM, stated that the introduction of FUSION technology is expected to improve traffic efficiency by 25 percent.

This technology aims to address congestion and delays that have affected bus services, which have seen reliability drop to 77 percent due to various issues, including a burst water main that caused major delays.

In addition to the new train services, the Bee Network is ramping up the electrification of Greater Manchester's buses, with 99 services now operated entirely by electric vehicles.

Councillors are also considering leaving space for the northern stretch of HS2 as part of future transport planning.

articles.title: Six arrests made in Middleton over £6 million cannabis importation scheme
articles.excerpt: Authorities arrested six individuals in Middleton as part of a sophisticated cannabis importation plan valued at nearly £6 million, involving a shipment from Canada.
articles.content_html:
Six individuals were arrested in Middleton on Wednesday night in connection with a sophisticated cannabis importation scheme valued at nearly £6 million. The operation involved transporting cannabis concealed within a large lumber shipment from Canada to the UK.

Canadian authorities replaced the cannabis with a synthetic product before it reached the UK. The individuals were observed interacting with the container, which raised suspicions and led to the arrests.

The cannabis was hidden within sophisticated concealments, indicating a well-planned operation.

As investigations continue, authorities are likely to assess the broader implications of this case on local drug-related issues and enforcement strategies.

The shipment was allowed to continue its journey to the UK and was tracked, resulting in officers from Greater Manchester Police’s Serious Organised Crime Group seizing a lorry at an address in Heywood Old Road in Middleton on Wednesday night. They remain in police custody for questioning. Police also recovered a significant amount of suspected Class A drugs at the address. Detective Inspector Rich McCorry, of GMP’s Serious Organised Crime Group, said: “This seizure demonstrates the strength of the relationships we have built with our international law enforcement partners and our continued commitment to tackling organised crime groups operating across international borders. “Working closely with the Canadian authorities, we were able to identify and disrupt an attempt to flood Greater Manchester’s communities with a significant quantity of cannabis worth almost £6 million. “I would like to thank our Canadian colleagues for their early notification and assistance with this investigation, without their help we would not have been able to take these drugs off our streets. “Organised criminal networks often believe they can operate beyond the reach of law enforcement. “Operations such as this show that intelligence sharing, partnership working and proactive policing can have a significant impact on criminality both nationally and internationally.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.excerpt: Ardan Hartley has been fined after dumping builders' rubble and bathroom furniture in a skip without a permit.
articles.content_html:
Ardan Hartley, of Halifax Road, Rochdale, has been ordered to pay £508 after illegally dumping builders' rubble and old bathroom furniture in a skip on a private driveway in Rossendale.

Hartley appeared at Burnley Magistrates' Court, where he pleaded guilty to two environmental offences. The court heard that on or around 29 July 2026, he deposited controlled waste in a skip without the necessary environmental permit.

Images provided by Rossendale Borough Council showed a skip filled with a cut-in-half bath, a toilet, bin bags, nails, paint tins, and various rubble materials. Hartley admitted to breaching the Environmental Protection Act 1990 by failing to obtain the required permit for waste disposal.

articles.title: Haider Ali jailed for 10 years and six months for managing drug supply in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Haider Ali has been sentenced to 10 years and six months for his role in an organised crime group supplying class A drugs in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Haider Ali has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for managing an organised crime group that supplied class A drugs across Rochdale.

The investigation into Ali began after police received information about a drug deal occurring from a car parked on Baron Street in Rochdale town centre just before midnight on 4 January 2025.

Officers followed the vehicle, and when it stopped at a petrol station, they executed a stop to prevent it from fleeing. Ali, a passenger in the car, attempted to walk away but was detained by officers.

During a search, Ali was found with over £1,000 in cash and two mobile phones. Further searches revealed bundles containing heroin and cocaine.

Ali was linked to the Adam drug line and was found to be managing street dealers, having progressed from being a street dealer himself in 2014 to a significant role within the organised crime group by 2024.

Evidence indicated that he directed other dealers on their operations.

The court's decision reflects the serious nature of Ali's crimes and the impact of drug supply on the community. Greater Manchester Police continue to target those involved in drug supply and organised crime to enhance community safety.
